source: Wang et al. (2023) Self-consistency improves chain of thought reasoning
finding: Founding LLM result: sample many reasoning paths and take the most frequent answer. This is the fixed-sample baseline every stopping rule is judged against.
numbers: Gains over greedy chain of thought: GSM8K +17.9, SVAMP +11.0, AQuA +12.2, StrategyQA +6.4, ARC-challenge +3.9 points (abstract).
limits: Budget (often 40 samples) is chosen by hand. The paper gives no rule for when fewer samples suffice.
agent_relevance: The vote is what a stopping rule monitors. Gains are large on arithmetic and small on commonsense, so the value of extra samples depends on the task.

source: Aggarwal et al. (2023) Adaptive-Consistency: Let's sample step by step
finding: Stops sampling when a Beta or Dirichlet posterior says the current majority will stay the majority. Spends samples where agreement is slow.
numbers: 17 datasets, 3 models. Up to 7.9x fewer samples (Boolean Expressions, no accuracy loss). Average accuracy drop under 0.1 points. Cap 40 samples, confidence threshold 0.95.
limits: The posterior check is repeated after every sample with no correction for repeated looks (the critique made by ConSol). Savings depend on how peaked the answer distribution is.
agent_relevance: Direct template for stop after enough agreement. A 0.95 threshold on majority stability is a ready default.

source: Aggarwal et al. (2023) Adaptive-Consistency, results by task type
finding: Savings are consistent across task families and nearly free in accuracy.
numbers: Samples vs fixed 40: MATH 13.8 (3.3x fewer, -0.1 acc); commonsense 15.8 (2.9x, -0.2); symbolic 13.1 (3.8x, +0.0); code 173.6 vs 312.5 (2.4x, +0.4). Accuracy: MATH 73.2 vs 73.1; commonsense 66.0 vs 65.8.
limits: Averages over datasets. Code uses a different sample cap (about 312 on average).
agent_relevance: Expect a 2.5 to 4x cost cut at equal accuracy as a first estimate for a majority-agreement stopper.

source: Aggarwal et al. (2023) Adaptive-Consistency, by model
finding: Weaker or more diffuse models save less because agreement arrives more slowly. Savings track model strength.
numbers: Fewer generations: GPT-3.5-Turbo 4.4x (10.0 vs 40, acc 76.4 vs 76.2); Vicuna-13B 1.9x (21.7 vs 40, acc 54.0 vs 54.1); Code-davinci-002 3.4x (49.4 vs 104.1, acc 69.8 vs 69.7).
limits: Only three models, all of 2023 vintage.
agent_relevance: A stop rule cuts less when the model is weak; a weak agent should expect to run closer to the cap.

source: Aggarwal et al. (2023) Adaptive-Consistency, stopping-rule ablation and equal-cost comparison
finding: At equal average cost, adaptive stopping beats fixed sampling, and the Beta rule beats simple Majority and Entropy rules. Random stopping is worst.
numbers: GSM8K at average cost 10 samples: about 3 points higher accuracy than fixed-n Self-Consistency (up to 5 points on other sets). Dirichlet and CRP match Beta but run about four orders of magnitude slower.
limits: Rules compared: Random, Majority, Entropy, Beta, Dirichlet, CRP. Gain is largest when the budget is small.
agent_relevance: Use a posterior-lead rule, not a bare k-votes-agree rule, when budget is tight.

source: Li et al. (2024) Escape sky-high cost: Early-Stopping Self-Consistency (ESC)
finding: Split the sample budget into windows and stop at the first window whose answers all agree. No prior knowledge of the model needed.
numbers: Fewer samples: MATH -33.8%, GSM8K -80.1%, StrategyQA -76.8%, CommonsenseQA -78.5%, Coin Flip -84.2%, Last Letters -67.4%, with comparable accuracy. Window 8 for MATH (cap 64), 5 for others (cap 40). Results averaged over 10 runs.
limits: Variance omitted in the paper. Window size is a hand choice. Heavy savings come on easy tasks.
agent_relevance: Cheapest possible stop rule: a full window of identical answers. It matches full voting while cutting up to 80%.

source: Li et al. (2024) ESC, scaling with cap size
finding: Accuracy equals full self-consistency at every cap, and savings grow with the cap. Saving depends strongly on model strength.
numbers: MATH, cap 64: GPT-4 SC 60.31 vs ESC 60.31 using 42.41 samples; GPT-3.5-Turbo 49.96 vs 49.96 using 52.37 samples; Llama-2-7b 7.70 vs 7.70 using 62.48 samples (almost no saving).
limits: Table text is partly garbled in PDF extraction; Table 2 values read directly.
agent_relevance: Very weak models get no saving because agreement never arrives. Same pattern as Adaptive-Consistency.

source: Li et al. (2024) ESC, cost-matched baseline
finding: Plain self-consistency given the same average number of samples as ESC does worse, so the gain is from stopping and not only from using fewer samples.
numbers: Authors report cost-matched SC loses accuracy following the usual sample-size curve; exact per-cell deltas not read reliably from the garbled Table 1.
quote: ESC can get higher accuracy under the same sampling costs.
limits: Direction stated in the text; exact numbers not verified.
agent_relevance: Report stopping results against cost-matched fixed sampling, not only against the full budget.

source: Lee et al. (2025) ConSol: SPRT to find consistent LLM reasoning paths
finding: Applies Wald's SPRT and a mixture SPRT to the top two answers (p = p1/(p1+p2), H0 p=0.5). Cites Type I error inflation from repeated peeking in Adaptive-Consistency. Samples 2-3 at a time in parallel.
numbers: Token reduction vs Self-Cons@40: AIME24 o3-mini-medium SPRT 84.8% (Ada-Cons 62.8%); GPQA Diamond o3-mini-low SPRT 86.2% (Ada-Cons 70.1%); GSM8K gpt-4o-mini mSPRT 88.7%. Accuracy: AIME24 o3-mini-low 70.0 vs 80.0 (SPRT); GPQA 68.2 vs 66.7 (SPRT) and 70.2 (mSPRT); GSM8K 94.2 vs 93.5 and 93.9.
limits: Cap raised to 256 against 40 for baselines, so some accuracy gain comes from extra samples on hard items. Parameters are extreme (p1=0.5001, beta about 0.95), so this is not a classical SPRT guarantee. Short-answer and multiple-choice tasks only. Part of the evaluation is simulated from a categorical fit to 40 samples.
agent_relevance: Best current evidence for SPRT-style stopping. Allow a high cap for contested items and stop early on clear ones.

source: Lee et al. (2025) ConSol, why an early no-consensus stop works
finding: When the top answer's share p1 is below 0.5, neither of the two top answers is usually right, so extra sampling is poor value. The test accepts H0 on weak evidence and stops.
numbers: Fig 1 and 2 on o3-mini low, medium and high with 40 samples each: most p1 values above 0.5; entropy falls with model strength.
limits: Stopping on no dominant answer costs hard-item accuracy if the model would have found the answer with more tries. ConSol raises the cap to 256 to offset.
agent_relevance: Two stop outcomes are useful: stop-confident and stop-give-up. Give-up should trigger a different action (re-plan, verify, escalate), not just stop.

source: Lee et al. (2025) ConSol, limitations stated by the authors
finding: Authors say results depend on sensitive parameter settings and that only short-answer and multiple-choice tasks were tested.
numbers: Code and PyPI package released (consol).
limits: No test on open-ended or long-form output; no independent replication found this session.
agent_relevance: Do not copy the extreme parameters blindly. Calibrate on logged items from our own tasks.

source: Morandi (2026) Sequential consensus for multi-agent LLM debates: Wald-SPRT compute governor
finding: SPRT on a judge's 0-1 consensus score after each debate round. It works only if the score separates useful from useless convergence.
numbers: GSM8K (200 items; gpt-5, claude-opus-4-6, gemini-2.5-pro agents): 1.01 average rounds, 4.06 calls, 97.0% accuracy vs fixed-5 debate 99.0% at 15 calls (3.7x fewer calls, -2 points). MMLU (200 items): hit the cap Rmax=8 on 99.5% of items, accuracy 94.2% vs 93.8%, cost 2.1x higher.
limits: n=200 per task; two-proportion standard error about 2.2 points, so the 2-point GSM8K drop is within noise. Calibration on 40 items. Independence across rounds is violated since later rounds see earlier ones.
agent_relevance: A stopper is only as good as its signal. Check calibration first. If the signal has no separation, the stopper should refuse to stop and warn.

source: Morandi (2026) SPRT debate governor, calibration and failure detection
finding: Calibrated KL divergence between score distributions for useful and not-yet-useful convergence is the diagnostic. Near-zero KL means the rule drifts to the cap.
numbers: On MMLU calibrated KL is about 0 and the score-stability check scores 50.1%, no better than chance. Simulation with Beta calibrations for MMLU, GSM8K, JudgeBench: rounds cut from 5.0 to 2.38, 2.61, 2.49; SPRT classification accuracy 98.3, 98.1, 98.2%. Loosening alpha to 0.20 saves one round and costs about 5 accuracy points.
limits: Simulation accuracy holds only under the assumed Beta models; real-LLM runs diverge on MMLU.
agent_relevance: Before trusting a stop rule on a new task, test that its signal separates right from wrong on a small labelled set.

source: Wan et al. (2024/2025) Reasoning-Aware Self-Consistency (RASC)
finding: Scores each sample for answer consistency and reasoning quality, stops when a weighted criterion is met, then weighted-votes. A rival to answer-only stopping.
numbers: 10 datasets (commonsense, math, symbolic): about 60-80% fewer samples with accuracy kept or improved; abstract says about 70%. Feature ablation: answer-only 10.86 generations / 55.5% (math); reasoning-only 5.50 / 50.4%; combined 8.20 / 55.8%. About 80% less inference time than SC.
limits: Reasoning-quality scoring adds overhead. Accuracy is lower with reasoning-only features, so reasoning scores alone are not enough.
agent_relevance: Answer agreement plus a rationale-quality check stops earlier than agreement alone and keeps accuracy.

source: Taubenfeld et al. (2025) Confidence improves self-consistency (CISC)
finding: Weight each vote by the model's own confidence. Weighted voting reaches the target accuracy with fewer samples, which is another route to stopping sooner.
numbers: Nine models, four datasets: required reasoning paths cut by over 40% on average. Gemma2-9B on MATH: 8 samples with CISC match 30-sample SC (73% cost reduction). P(True) confidence works best; the best-calibrated method was the least useful.
limits: This uses a fixed lower N, not a sequential test. What matters is within-question discrimination, not calibration across questions.
agent_relevance: Calibration across questions is the wrong test for confidence. Ask whether confidence ranks right above wrong answers on the same question.

source: Fu et al. (2025) Deep Think with Confidence (DeepConf)
finding: Uses internal token confidence to drop weak traces and stop generation early. Adds a consensus stop on top of a 16-trace warmup.
numbers: AIME 2025, GPT-OSS-120B at 512 traces: up to 99.9% accuracy with up to 84.7% fewer tokens. Consensus-threshold ablation, Qwen3-32B on AIME24: tau=0.95 keeps accuracy exactly while saving 15.4% and 52.8% of tokens at budget 32 and 512 (low variant), 22.0% and 54.7% (high variant).
limits: Tau=0.90 and 0.85 save up to 69.6% of tokens but lose up to 0.26 and 0.47 points in the low variant. Authors list high confidence on wrong traces as a key limitation.
agent_relevance: A 0.95 majority-share stop after a 16-sample warmup is a tested default. Confident wrong answers cap what any agreement stop can catch.

source: Huang et al. (2025) Efficient test-time scaling via self-calibration
finding: Trains the model to give calibrated confidence in one pass, then uses it for early stopping in best-of-N and confidence-weighted voting.
numbers: 3 LLMs, 6 datasets. MathQA: early stopping lifts accuracy from 81.0 to 83.6 at a 16-response budget. Figure 1 (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct): confidence-weighted SC saves 39.8%, 50.4% and 94.2% of samples at matched accuracy points.
limits: Needs a training step (distilling SC confidence), so it is not a pure scaffold. Authors say raw LLM confidence is overconfident.
agent_relevance: Raw self-confidence is unreliable for stopping; agreement-derived confidence is the sturdier signal.

source: Chen et al. (2024) Are more LM calls all you need? Scaling of Vote systems
finding: Boundary condition: more votes can hurt. On a mix of easy and hard questions, majority-vote accuracy can rise and then fall as calls increase.
numbers: Inverse-U in accuracy vs number of calls observed on MMLU Physics, TruthfulQA, GPQA and AVeriTeC (exact peak positions not recorded). More calls help easy queries and hurt hard queries. The model predicts the best number of calls from a small sample.
limits: Theory assumes per-query correct-answer probabilities and shows U or inverse-U depending on the mix. Not a stopping-rule test.
agent_relevance: If the modal answer on a hard item is wrong, more agreement only strengthens the error. Add a diversity or verifier step for hard items.

source: Brown et al. (2024) Large Language Monkeys: repeated sampling
finding: Coverage keeps rising with samples, but picking the right one without a verifier stalls. Majority vote and reward models plateau.
numbers: SWE-bench Lite with DeepSeek-Coder-V2-Instruct: 15.9% solved with 1 sample, 56% with 250 samples (single-sample state of the art 43%). Without verifiers, majority voting and reward models plateau beyond several hundred samples.
limits: Coverage is an oracle measure; real gains need a verifier. Code and proofs have cheap verifiers, word problems do not.
agent_relevance: Where a cheap check exists (tests, proof checker), stop on the first verified pass, not on agreement.

source: Snell et al. (2024) Scaling LLM test-time compute optimally
finding: The best use of extra test-time compute depends on question difficulty. Compute-optimal allocation beats a fixed best-of-N baseline.
numbers: Compute-optimal scaling beats best-of-N using about 4x less test-time compute; a smaller model with extra test-time compute can beat a 14x larger model in some settings (intro).
limits: Difficulty is estimated with model-based bins; gains vary by difficulty level.
agent_relevance: Stopping rule and difficulty estimate are two sides of one decision. Estimate difficulty from early agreement.

source: Johari, Pekelis, Walsh (2019) Always valid inference: continuous monitoring of A/B tests
finding: Checking a fixed-sample test repeatedly and stopping at the first success inflates false positives. mSPRT-based always-valid p-values fix this at small cost in run-time.
numbers: With 10,000 samples Type I error can easily increase fivefold. The mixture SPRT has average run-length about 20% better than fixed-horizon for most settings and up to 40% better in some. Missing the effect-size prior by two orders of magnitude gives about a 20% drop in power and a 40% rise in run-length. Used on hundreds of thousands of experiments at Optimizely.
quote: Very high false positive probabilities are obtained, well in excess of the nominal alpha.
limits: Assumes independent samples and a known effect-size family. LLM samples at fixed temperature on one problem are not fully independent.
agent_relevance: Plain check-after-every-sample majority stops are peeking. Use a mixture test or a high threshold to keep error honest.

source: Howard, Ramdas, McAuliffe, Sekhon (2021) Time-uniform confidence sequences
finding: Confidence sequences are valid at all times at once. They generalise Wald's SPRT to nonparametric cases and match the law-of-the-iterated-logarithm rate.
numbers: Width rate O(sqrt(log log t / t)), matching the LIL lower bound. Links Cramer-Chernoff bounds, the LIL and the SPRT.
limits: Theory paper with no LLM tests. Constants are loose at small n.
agent_relevance: Gives a valid way to stop on agreement when the answer distribution is unknown.

source: Wald (1945) Sequential tests of statistical hypotheses; Wald and Wolfowitz (1948) Optimum character of the SPRT
finding: Not read this session (access blocked). From memory: the SPRT multiplies likelihood ratios and stops at two thresholds, about (1-beta)/alpha and beta/(1-alpha). Wald and Wolfowitz proved it has the smallest expected sample size under both H0 and H1 among all tests with the same error bounds.
numbers: From memory only: expected sample size often cited as about half that of the best fixed-sample test at equal error rates.
limits: Optimality holds for i.i.d. observations and two simple hypotheses; expected size can be large for true values between H0 and H1; truncation is needed in practice.
agent_relevance: LLM samples are not truly i.i.d. and hypotheses are not simple, so the optimality does not carry over automatically.

source: Armitage, McPherson, Rowe (1969) Repeated significance tests on accumulating data
finding: Not read this session. From memory: looking at accumulating data repeatedly at the nominal 5% level raises the real false-positive rate far above 5%.
numbers: From memory, roughly 14% after 5 looks and 19% after 10 looks at nominal 5%.
limits: Numbers need checking before citation.
agent_relevance: Same warning as ConSol on peeking.

source: Pocock (1977) group sequential methods; Bassler et al. (2010) trials stopped early for benefit
finding: Not read this session. From memory: Pocock used a constant stricter nominal level per look (about 0.0158 for 5 looks). Bassler found trials stopped early for benefit report larger effects than matched complete trials.
numbers: From memory only: ratio of relative risks about 0.71 (95% CI 0.65 to 0.77), bias larger with fewer events.
limits: Check numbers before citing.
agent_relevance: Early stopping on a lucky streak overstates confidence; estimates taken at the stopping point are biased upward.

source: ConSol (2025) vs Adaptive-Consistency (2023): rival designs
finding: Posterior-lead stopping (Adaptive-Consistency) versus likelihood-ratio stopping (SPRT). SPRT gets higher token reduction at equal accuracy, but with a 256 cap and tuned parameters.
numbers: AIME24 o3-mini-high token reduction: Ada-Cons 64.6%, SPRT 84.5%, mSPRT 82.2%, p-value test 54.0%; accuracy 96.7% for all. GSM gpt-4o-mini: Ada-Cons 82.8%, SPRT 88.6%.
limits: Different caps (40 vs 256) and different model families from the 2023 paper, so not a clean head-to-head. One run per cell.
agent_relevance: The two stop styles differ by 5 to 20 points of savings; no evidence yet on which is more robust off the benchmarks.

source: Competing explanations for why agreement stopping works (synthesis of the sources above)
finding: Two accounts: (1) correct answers are drawn more often than wrong ones, so the mode is stable early (Wang, Aggarwal, ConSol); (2) difficulty varies, so easy items agree quickly and hard ones fail either way (Chen, Snell).
numbers: Chen shows the inverse-U arises from the easy and hard mix; ConSol shows that when p1 < 0.5 the mode is rarely right; DeepConf notes confident wrong traces.
limits: No experiment in these sources cleanly separates the two accounts. They predict different things only on hard items whose modal answer is wrong.
agent_relevance: Test the stop rule on items where the modal answer is wrong and measure how often it fires.
